title: Quotations for Chapter 20 (Say's law and the general glut): Say's chapter 'Des Débouchés' (1803) and its English translation (1821), with Say's Letters to Malthus (1821); Malthus's Principles (1820); Ricardo's Principles (1817, ch. XIX) and his letters to Malthus (1814-1821); Sismondi's Nouveaux principes (1819); Walras (1874) on the offer and demand of two commodities; Lange (1942), who named 'Walras' law' and distinguished it from Say's law; J. S. Mill's essay of 1829-30 on consumption and production; the boom and crisis of 1825 in Tooke's History of Prices (1838, vol. II) and in English (1827), with the foreign loans contracted in London in 1824 and 1825; Reinhart and Rogoff (2008) on the Latin American defaults of the 1820s; Baumol (1999) on the name of the law
source: J.-B. Say, Traité d'économie politique (Paris, 1803), first edition, and A Treatise on Political Economy, tr. C. R. Prinsep (London, 1821), and Letters to Mr. Malthus (London, 1821), on archive.org; T. R. Malthus, Principles of Political Economy (London, 1820), on archive.org; D. Ricardo, On the Principles of Political Economy, and Taxation (London, 1817), first edition, and J. Bonar (ed.), Letters of David Ricardo to Thomas Robert Malthus (1887), Project Gutenberg eBooks 33310 and 36345; J.-C.-L. Simonde de Sismondi, Nouveaux principes d'économie politique, tome I (Paris, 1819), on archive.org; L. Walras, Éléments d'économie politique pure (Lausanne, 1874), on archive.org; O. Lange, 'Say's Law: A Restatement and Criticism' (1942), on archive.org; J. S. Mill, Essays on Some Unsettled Questions of Political Economy (1844), Project Gutenberg eBook 12004; T. Tooke, A History of Prices, vol. II (1838), on archive.org; H. English, A Complete View of the Joint Stock Companies formed during the years 1824 and 1825 (1827), on archive.org; C. M. Reinhart and K. S. Rogoff, NBER Working Paper 13882 (2008); W. J. Baumol, 'Retrospectives: Say's Law', Journal of Economic Perspectives 13(1), 1999, the abstract on the AEA's website
series: id, dynasty (place), year, year_note, value (numbers in the quotation, ';'-separated; fractions as a/b, mixed numbers as n+a/b), unit, numeral (unused), file (key of 'sources'), juan (location: printed page, chapter or letter; the PDF page for the image rows), quote (verbatim, as in the document's text, or a transcription for the image rows, with the columns separated by ' | '), note
license: Quotations for criticism and teaching, each with its source. Say (1803, 1821), Malthus (1820), Ricardo (1817) and his letters (Bonar 1887), Sismondi (1819), Walras (1874), Mill (1844), Tooke (1838) and English (1827) are in the public domain; the Project Gutenberg texts are used under the Project Gutenberg licence (no Project Gutenberg trademark is used here), and the archive.org texts are OCR of public-domain scans. Lange (1942): 'Copyright 1942 by the University of Chicago'; five short passages are quoted. Reinhart and Rogoff (2008): '© 2008 by Carmen M. Reinhart and Kenneth S. Rogoff. All rights reserved. Short sections of text, not to exceed two paragraphs, may be quoted without explicit permission provided that full credit, including © notice, is given to the source.' Baumol (1999): three phrases of the abstract on the American Economic Association's article page. The chapter's Chinese renders the English and French; the translations are the book's.
fetch: data/fetch/verify_web_quotes.py (rows citing say1803, say1821, saylet1821, malthus1820, ricardo1817, ricardo_letters, sismondi1819, walras1874, lange1942, jsmill1844, tooke1838v2, english1827, rr2008tid and baumol1999; the english1827img rows are read on the page image); checks/check_ch20.py (the readings and every quotation of the text)
notes: Say. The first edition (1803) is quoted in French for the chapter's core sentences (rows sy03_*); its OCR keeps the space before commas and the line-end hyphen of 'dé- bouchés', quoted as it reads. Prinsep translated the fourth edition (1819); the English rows (sy21_*) give the later Say, who added the footnotes on hoarding, on France in 1811-1813 and on Brazil, and the reservation that 'one product' can be raised in too great abundance in relation to all others (row sy21_notmaintain). The note on Sismondi, Malthus and Ricardo (row sy21_prinsep) is the translator's (marked T.), not Say's. Malthus (1820). The OCR garbles a few words near the quoted passages ('abe' for 'at which', 'ynsume' for 'consume'); the rows stop before them or quote them as they read. Malthus's footnote names James Mill's reply to Spence (Commerce Defended, 1808) as the source of the doctrine that 'one half' of commodities furnishes a market for the other half (row ml_mill). Ricardo's letters. Bonar numbers the letters; the rows give the number, the place and the date printed at the head of each letter. Sismondi (1819). The OCR drops most accents and misreads some letters ('eclaireis' for 'éclaircis', '& leurs yeux' for 'à leurs yeux'); the rows quote it as it reads, and the chapter quotes the French with the accents restored. The hats of livre II, ch. VI (a hat factory of Lyon that made 100,000 hats in 1817 and 110,000 in 1818, or made 100,000 and sold 90,000) are Sismondi's illustration in his reply to a passage of Ricardo's ch. VII, not a statistic. Walras (1874). Section 45 states that to demand 200 hectolitres of oats at the price of ½ in wheat is to offer 100 hectolitres of wheat (the OCR reads the fraction ½ as '-^'); §46 draws the conclusion for two commodities. Lange (1942) gives Walras's identity its name (row lg_walras) and distinguishes it from Say's law; Lange's own phrase for the weaker form is 'an equation which holds only in equilibrium' (row lg_equation). Mill. The preface dates the essays to 1829 and 1830; Essay II was published in 1844. Tooke (1838), vol. II. The passages of pp. 150-152 are quotations from the Annual Register for 1824, which Tooke prints in footnotes; the 'eight times' leverage of a £100 share with £5 paid at a premium of £40 is the Annual Register's example (row tk2_eight). The 770 country bankers and 63 failures are from Mr. Ridley's speech in the House of Commons of 3 June 1828, quoted by Tooke (row tk2_ridley). The box of one-pound notes (row tk2_box) is told in a footnote: the Bank found a box of about £600,000 or £700,000 in one-pound notes that had not been destroyed and issued them in the panic. English (1827). The text (pp. 30-31) gives the companies formed or projected in 1824 and 1825 and the foreign loans; the table of the foreign loans (p. 42) is read on the page image (rows en_l24_*, en_l25_*, en_l24_total, en_l25_total). In the table, 'Cont. Price' is the price at which the contractor took the loan, per £100 of nominal capital, and 'Money advanced' is the nominal capital times that price; two rows do not agree with the rule: Denmark (75½ printed, but £2,718,750 is 75 per cent of £3,625,000) and Guatemala (73 per cent of £1,428,571 is £1,042,857, not £1,042,988); both column totals add the printed figures. Reinhart and Rogoff (2008). Table 3 lists, by country, the year of independence (for the countries independent in the nineteenth century) and the years of external default or rescheduling in four columns, 1800-1824, 1825-1849, 1850-1874 and 1875-1899; the rows rr_t3_* quote the name, the year of independence and the column 1825-1849 (for Brazil, whose only entry is 1898, the column 1875-1899); Table 8 lists the crises at the financial centre (rows rr_t8_*). The PDF's text is searched in pdftotext's normal and -layout output.
